tags.label: Metaphor
tags.reasoning: Jude compares the presence of the false teachers at fellowship meals to spots or blemishes that ruin the appearance of the gathering.

tags.label: Other images
tags.reasoning: Describing the false teachers as spots in the love feasts is a visual image of moral and communal corruption.

tags.label: Metaphor
tags.reasoning: Jude speaks of God's ability to keep them from stumbling as if it were a physical act of preventing someone from falling on a path.

tags.label: Path and journey
tags.reasoning: The reference to falling implies a journey or a path that believers are walking upon.

tags.label: woe oracle
tags.reasoning: The verse explicitly begins with the interjection 'Woe' followed by a description of the divine judgement awaiting the opponents.

tags.label: closing and benediction
tags.reasoning: The letter concludes with a doxology and blessing typical of the closing section of New Testament epistles.

tags.label: scripture-shaped (midrashic)
tags.reasoning: The text explicitly invokes the figures of Cain, Balaam, and Korah to classify the false teachers. Proposed by: Bauckham, R. J., Jude, 2 Peter, 1983.

tags.label: scripture-shaped (midrashic)
tags.reasoning: Jude quotes directly from 1 Enoch to bolster his argument, framing the contemporary opponents within the apocalyptic prophecy of the ancestor. Proposed by: Charles, J. D., Jude, 2008.

tags.label: hymnic or liturgical
tags.reasoning: The concluding doxology utilizes established early Christian liturgical language to praise God.

tags.label: Chiasm of the Body of the Letter
tags.reasoning: Some scholars propose that the body of the letter (verses 5-16) forms a chiasm centered on the description of the false teachers in verses 8-10, flanked by judgment examples (5-7 and 11-13) and prophecy (14-16). Proposed by: Richard Bauckham, Jude, 2 Peter (Word Biblical Commentary), 1983.

tags.label: The Exodus wilderness generation as a type of false believers within the Church
tags.reasoning: Jude uses the destruction of those who did not believe after being saved from Egypt as an explicit historical type to warn the recipients about the apostates in their own midst. Proposed by: Douglas Moo, The Letter of Jude (The Pillar New Testament Commentary), 2023.

tags.label: The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah as a type of the judgment of false teachers
tags.reasoning: Jude calls the destruction of these cities an 'example' (Greek: deigma) of the eternal fire that awaits the ungodly teachers infiltrating the community. Proposed by: Gene L. Green, Jude and 2 Peter (Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament), 2008.
